The 1970 Bhola cyclone struck the East Pakistan coast on 12 November and killed an estimated 300,000 people, and eleven East Pakistani leaders charged the government with gross neglect.

On the night of 25 March 1971 the Pakistan Army began Operation Searchlight, a planned pacification meant to take the major cities and eliminate all opposition within a month. Foreign journalists were deported beforehand, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was arrested. Major Ziaur Rahman broadcast the declaration of independence from the radio station at Chittagong on 26 March. Resistance grew as Bengali soldiers defected and merged into the Mukti Bahini, supplied from India, while Pakistan raised the Razakar, Al-Badr and Al-Shams militias.

India joined the war on 3 December after Pakistani air strikes on northern India. Indian aircraft achieved near-total air supremacy within a week, and the East Pakistan ports were blockaded. On 16 December 1971 the Pakistani commander in East Pakistan signed the Instrument of Surrender in Dhaka, and over 93,000 Pakistani troops surrendered, the largest surrender since the Second World War.

The Pakistani military and supporting militias carried out widespread killings, deportation and rape. Estimates range from 300,000 to 3,000,000 killed and from 200,000 to 400,000 women raped. On 14 December 1971 the army and the Razakars seized at least 100 physicians, professors, writers and engineers in Dacca and murdered them. An estimated 10 million refugees fled to India and 30 million were internally displaced.

Bhutan was the first state to recognise Bangladesh, on 6 December 1971. The Simla Agreement of 1972 between India and Pakistan secured Pakistani recognition of Bangladesh in exchange for the return of prisoners of war. In West Pakistan the defeat discredited Yahya Khan's rule. The war changed the geopolitical landscape of South Asia and became an episode of Cold War tension involving the United States, the Soviet Union and China.
banjarmasin: Banjarmasin lies on a delta island near the confluence of the Barito and Martapura rivers, and the Martapura bisects it. The land is flat and low-lying, and several smaller rivers affected by the tides form its drainage. The city sits in a swampy region, generally below water level, and is prone to flooding by tidal bores. Its climate is tropical monsoon, with heavy rain from November to June.

The name is thought to be a corruption of Bandar Masih, Port Masih, after Patih Masih, who ruled the port and surrounding villages. Dayaks from the interior visited the port to trade, and some settled there.Europeans first met the Banjar through trade, mostly at Banten from 1596. Dutch traders came to the port only after Banten's rulers banned them. On 17 July 1607 the Sultan took revenge on a Dutch ship at Banjarmasin by hijacking it and massacring the crew. A trade agreement gave the Dutch East India Company a monopoly of trade in the port, but the sultan expelled the company in 1638 after waging war and burning much of its property around the port.

The Imperial Japanese Army occupied the city in the Second World War, and control then passed to the Imperial Japanese Navy, whose rule locals described as harsher. Australian forces liberated the city in September 1945. The people opposed the return of Dutch rule, which led to the four-year Kalimantan Physical Revolution between Indonesian nationalists and the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, ending with Dutch recognition of Indonesia in 1949. The city was granted city status in 1959 and became the capital of the new province of South Kalimantan.

Banjarmasin is the largest city in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, and the centre of Banjarese culture. The provincial capital was legally moved to Banjarbaru on 15 February 2022. The culture of the Banjar people is described as a river culture, influenced by Dayak, Javanese, Malay, Arab and even Persian peoples, and keeps elements of a Hindu-Buddhist past despite a Muslim majority.
bank-of-england: After the Revolution of 1688 brought William III and Mary II to the throne, a national bank became possible. During the Nine Years' War the Royal Navy was defeated by the French at the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690, and the government decided to rebuild it, but low public funds and poor credit made it impossible to borrow the £1.5 million it wanted. The idea of a public bank was two decades old. John Locke was an early supporter and, once it was set up, an early investor, and in 1691 the Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a national bank to bolster public finances. It was chartered in 1694.

The Ways and Means Act of 1715 authorised the bank to take subscriptions for a government issue of 5% annuities meant to raise £910,000; this began its role in managing government stocks, which it kept until 1998. The bank has been on Threadneedle Street since 1734, and a satirical cartoon by James Gillray in 1797 gave it the nickname the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street. Its first branches opened in 1826, and by 1829 there were eleven; the last five closed in 1997.

Britain was on the gold standard until 1931, when the Great Depression forced the bank to take it off. Banknotes were issued from 1694, hand-written at first and fully printed from 1855. After the First World War the bank withdrew increasingly from private and commercial accounts to concentrate on central banking. It was privately owned by stockholders until its nationalisation in 1946 by the Attlee ministry.

The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and the model on which most modern central banks have been based. It is the world's second oldest central bank, after Sweden's of 1668. In 1998 it became an independent public body, and the Debt Management Office took over government debt. The bank is custodian of the official gold reserves of the United Kingdom and holds a monopoly on issuing banknotes in England and Wales.
banska-stiavnica: Banská Štiavnica stands in the middle of an immense caldera created by the collapse of an ancient volcano, known for its size as the Štiavnica Mountains. Its fate has been closely linked to the exploitation of abundant silver ore. Excavations show that the site was settled in the Neolithic period. The Slavic population named the settlement in the valley Štiavnica, meaning acidic stream, and the settlement on the hill above came to be called Bánya, the mine.

The first mining settlement was founded by Celts in the 3rd century BCE, probably by the Cotini tribe. The site was called terra banensium, the land of miners, as early as 1156. Skilled German settlers began arriving in the 13th century and adapted the local name to Schemnitz. Banská Štiavnica gained the status of a royal town in 1238, one of the first in the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the High and Late Middle Ages it was the main producer of silver and gold in the kingdom.

During the Ottoman Wars the town built powerful fortifications, including two castles, in the 16th century. It was also a centre of mining innovation: in 1627 gunpowder was used in a mine there, one of the first uses in the world. In the 18th century local scientists, among them Jozef Karol Hell, Maximilian Hell and Samuel Mikovíny, designed a system of reservoirs and channels called tajchy to drain flooded mines.

Samuel Mikovíny founded a Mining Academy in 1735, the first mining school in the Kingdom of Hungary. From 1763 it became the Academy of Mining with the support of Queen Maria Theresa, and in 1848 the Academy of Mining and Forestry, described as the first technical university in the world. In 1782 the town was the third biggest in the kingdom, but mining declined progressively from the second half of the 19th century.

Banská Štiavnica is a town in central Slovakia with a population of less than 10,000. The surviving urban centre was formed during the 16th century, and the town and its surroundings were proclaimed a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 11 December 1993. Sixty reservoirs were built between the 15th and 18th centuries, connected by more than 100 kilometres of channels, and they are now used mainly for recreation. The old and new castles have become museums.
banten: Banten lies at the western tip of Java. It is bordered by the Java Sea on the north, the Sunda Strait on the west and the Indian Ocean on the south, and by West Java and Jakarta on the east. The Sunda Strait carries sea lanes linking Australia and New Zealand with Southeast Asia, and Banten forms a link between Java and Sumatra. The province covers 9,355.76 square kilometres and ranges from sea level to 2,000 metres, with lowlands in the north and south and hills in the centre.

In the fourth and fifth centuries the area belonged to the kingdom of Tarumanagara. A Sanskrit inscription found in 1947 in Munjul describes life under Purnawarman. After Tarumanagara fell to an attack by Srivijaya, western Java became part of the Sunda Kingdom. Islam began to spread in the 15th century and by the late 16th century had replaced Hinduism and Buddhism as the main religion, with the establishment of the Banten Sultanate. According to the Babad Banten, Sunan Gunung Jati and Maulana Hasanuddin spread Islam widely.

The Portuguese were established in Banten before the Dutch, and the English, French and Danish also traded there. The Portuguese left in 1601 after the Dutch destroyed their fleet off the coast. The Dutch East India Company gradually weakened the sultanate, and on 22 November 1808 Governor-General Herman Willem Daendels declared it absorbed into the Dutch East Indies. Japan occupied the region from March 1942 and built the Saketi-Bayah railway to carry brown coal, using about 1,000 forced labourers, rōmusha, drawn mainly from Banten; casualties are estimated at 20,000 to 60,000, not counting mine workers. Banten became a separate province on 17 October 2000.

The capital of the province is Serang and its largest city is Tangerang. Most residents are Muslims, and the Bantenese, at 47 per cent, are the largest ethnic group. The Baduy people of Kanekes practise Sunda Wiwitan and keep their ancestral customs. The Great Mosque of Banten and Ujung Kulon National Park, a sanctuary of the Javan rhinoceros, are among its notable sites.
bantu-peoples: The Bantu peoples are a grouping of about 400 distinct Indigenous African ethnic groups who speak Bantu languages, of which there are between 440 and 680 depending on how language and dialect are defined. They are not a single ethnic group. The term Bantu is an artificial one, introduced into modern scholarship by Wilhelm Bleek in 1857 or 1858, based on a reconstructed Proto-Bantu word for people. Proto-Bantu is estimated to have been spoken 4,000 to 3,000 years ago in the area of modern Cameroon. The spread of Bantu speakers across Central, East and Southern Africa, the Bantu expansion, took roughly two millennia, during the 1st millennium BCE and the 1st millennium CE.

In the course of the expansion Bantu-speaking peoples absorbed or displaced many earlier inhabitants. Central African Pygmy groups, the Hadza of northern Tanzania and various Khoisan populations of southern Africa remained. Genetic analysis shows admixture with earlier local populations, and interaction with Cushitic, Nilotic and Central Sudanic speakers. Pioneering groups had reached parts of KwaZulu-Natal before the 3rd century CE and the Northern Cape by 500 CE.

Between the 9th and 15th centuries Bantu-speaking states began to emerge in the Great Lakes region and in the savanna south of the Central African rainforest, and from the 12th century state formation became more frequent. Examples include the Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba Empire, the Lunda Empire, Buganda, Rwanda and the Zulu Kingdom. The Monomotapa kings built the Great Zimbabwe complex, ancestral to the Shona. On the East African coast contact with Arab and Persian traders produced Swahili culture, whose language holds many Arabic loanwords.

Speakers of Bantu languages number in the hundreds of millions, roughly 350 million in the mid-2010s, about 30 per cent of Africa's population. About 90 million are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo alone.

In South Africa the term Bantu came into use in the 1920s in preference to Native. After World War II the National Party governments adopted it officially, and it became identified with apartheid, which named its eleven rural reserves Bantustans. It is now used there only in its linguistic sense.
bar-le-duc: Bar-le-Duc, formerly known as Bar, is the capital of the Meuse département in the Grand Est region of north-eastern France. The lower town, the more modern and busier part, extends along a narrow valley shut in by wooded or vine-clad hills, and the Ornain runs through it. The upper town, the Ville Haute, lies on the left bank of a small arm of the river, the Canal des Usines.

Bar-le-Duc was the seat of a county and, from 1354, of the Duchy of Bar. The town is probably of ancient origin but was unimportant until the 10th century, when Frederick I of Upper Lorraine fortified it. Bar was an independent duchy from 1354 to 1480, when the Duchy of Lorraine acquired it.

In 1916, during the Battle of Verdun, Bar-le-Duc was the assembly point for the supplies sent to the besieged city of Verdun. Thousands of trucks carrying men, equipment and food travelled north around the clock on the road linking the two towns, which the writer and politician Maurice Barres named the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, in April 1916.

The Ville Haute is crossed by a long, quiet street lined with houses of the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries, and holds 16th-century remains of the château of the dukes of Bar, dismantled in 1670. The church of Saint-Étienne contains the Cadaver Tomb of René of Châlon, who died in 1544, a carved white stone effigy of a half-decayed corpse by the 16th-century artist Ligier Richier. Among the natives of Bar-le-Duc are Mary of Guise, mother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and the mathematician Henri Poincaré. Bar-le-Duc jelly, made from currants and first mentioned in 1344, is known as Bar caviar.
bar-montenegro: Bar lies on the Adriatic shore in the coastal region of Montenegro, about 53 kilometres from Podgorica, with Lake Skadar, the largest lake in southern Europe, to the east. Its name is thought to be a shortened Slavic form of Antivari, from the Latin Antibarum or Antibari, meaning opposite Bari, for its position across the Adriatic from that Italian city. It is called Tivari in Albanian. Finds from the Neolithic show that people lived there in prehistoric times, and the name Antibarium is first quoted in the 10th century.

In the Middle Ages Bar was linked to the Slavic state of Duklja. Stefan Vojislav, ruler from 1018 to 1043, defeated the Byzantines in a battle on a hill near Bar and made it his seat. His son Mihailo I established the Archdiocese of Antivari, founded in 1089. Byzantium held the town from 1166 to 1183, until Stefan Nemanja conquered and destroyed it. The Nemanjić dynasty ruled it until 1360, then the Balšić family. The Venetians controlled Bar from 1405 to 1412, when it grew most and became a city-state, with its own Statute of Communes and coinage. They ruled again from 1443 to 1571, until the Ottomans captured Antivari and held it until 1878.

The Ottomans ceded Antivari to Montenegro at the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, and the town was made militarily neutral. In the late 1850s it had 4,000 inhabitants, 62.5 per cent of them Muslims; more than half left or were expelled after 1878. On 30 August 1904 Guglielmo Marconi made a radio link between Antivari and Bari, and in 1908 the first railway in this part of the Balkans opened there. In 1914 and 1915 Austro-Hungarian ships bombarded the port, and on 16 August 1914 a French fleet sank the cruiser SMS Zenta off the town in the Battle of Antivari. Bar joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918.

The old town of Stari Bar and the newer settlement by the sea are distinct: the district of Pristan was demolished in 1976 to enlarge the port, and its people moved mostly to Topolica. The Port of Bar and the Belgrade–Bar railway, opened in 1976, are the basis of its economy. King Nikola's castle at Topolica, built in 1885, houses the Bar Homeland Museum. Bar is the birthplace of Saint Jovan Vladimir, and has Orthodox and Catholic churches and mosques built by the Ottomans.
barbed-wire: Fencing of flat, thin wire with bristling points was first proposed in France by Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans in 1860. In April 1865 Louis François Janin proposed a double wire with diamond-shaped metal barbs. In 1867 alone six patents were issued, only two of them for livestock, one to Lucien B. Smith of Ohio, regarded as the American inventor. After the Civil War the plains were extensively settled, and ranchers, railroads and farmers all needed to fence large open spaces where wood and stone were costly and hedges unreliable.

In 1873 Joseph Glidden, a farmer, saw at a fair in DeKalb, Illinois a display by Henry B. Rose of a wooden strip with metallic points. With the hardware dealer Isaac L. Ellwood and the lumber merchant Jacob Haish he began experimenting, twisting two wires round the barbs with a grindstone and shaping barbs with a coffee mill. Glidden applied for a patent in October 1873; Haish, who held patents of his own, accused him of interference, and approval of Glidden's wire, nicknamed The Winner, was deferred until 24 November 1874.

In 1876 John Warne Gates demonstrated the wire in Military Plaza, San Antonio, showing cattle held by it, and sales rose sharply. Between 1873 and 1899 as many as 150 companies made barbed wire, then consolidated, notably into the American Steel and Wire Company, later part of U.S. Steel. A US District Court upheld the Glidden patent in 1880 and the Supreme Court affirmed it in 1892. Wire cut the cost of enclosing land and set farmers against open-range ranchers in the range wars. Heavy penalties were set for cutting fences, and some historians date the end of the Old West to the wire's spread.

Portuguese troops used barbed wire in the Battle of Magul in 1895, and it was used extensively in the Boer War, where it held the captured Boer population in concentration camps. In the First World War all combatants placed entanglements before their trenches to halt charges or funnel soldiers into machine-gun fire. The tank defeated it, as the Allied breakthrough at Amiens on 8 August 1918 showed.

Barbed wire is still the standard fencing for enclosing cattle in most regions of the United States. Fences are built between heavy braced posts and kept under great tension, often up to half a ton. The wire is galvanized, and high-tensile wire is thinner but resists stretching better. Razor wire, which replaces the barbs with near-continuous cutting surfaces, is used where humans must be kept out.
barbuda: Barbuda lies north of Antigua and covers about 160 square kilometres. Coral limestone makes up most of the island, which has very little variety in its landscape. Hills in the Barbuda Highlands on the eastern side reach about 38 metres, while the northwest corner holds many lagoons, and Codrington Lagoon dominates the western part. Salty ponds and scrubland are spread across the interior. The climate is tropical marine. Codrington, which grew up as the main residential area by 1666, is still the only town and the main settlement.

The first settlers arrived by canoe, as hunter-gatherers, around 2,900 to 3,000 BCE. Sources disagree on whether they came from South America, the Greater Antilles or the Yucatán region. They made cutting blades, hoes and picks from the shells of conch, trumpet and whelk. They were followed by Arawak people, present on Barbuda and Antigua from at least 1,000 BCE, whose numbers on Barbuda peaked between 1,500 and 800 years ago. They probably came from present-day Venezuela and Guyana, grew sweet potatoes, corn, cotton and tobacco, and made pottery in the Saladoid style, with white-on-red designs.

English colonisation was attempted from St. Kitts under a patent of 1625 granted to the Earl of Carlisle, and the island appears there as Barbado. In 1668 about 240 Kalinago attacked the 20 English inhabitants, and eight settlers died. Strong Kalinago resistance and drought caused this attempt to fail. In 1685 the crown granted the island to the brothers John and Christopher Codrington. The colonisers intended Barbuda to be a colony for the forced reproduction of enslaved people, but this never went through. Slavery was abolished there in 1834. Because a single land grant had covered the whole island, Barbudans went on farming communal property on their own account.

Barbuda forms part of the twin-island state of Antigua and Barbuda as an autonomous entity. It gained autonomy in 1976 through the Barbuda Local Government Act, which created the Barbuda Council, and gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1981 as part of Antigua and Barbuda. The Council has eleven members and sits in Codrington. Under the Barbuda Land Acts, land is held communally. The 2011 census counted 1,634 people. Fishing, especially for lobster, supplies most exports, and tourist attractions include the Frigate Bird Sanctuary in Codrington Lagoon, a 19th-century Martello Tower and the ruins of Highland House, the Codrington family home.
barcelona: Barcelona lies on the north-east coast of the Iberian Peninsula, facing the Mediterranean Sea, on a plain about 5 km wide limited by the Collserola mountain range, the Llobregat river to the south-west and the Besòs river to the north. It lies 120 km south of the Pyrenees. The escarpment of Montjuïc overlooks the harbour and is topped by Montjuïc Castle, a fortress built in the 17th and 18th centuries to control the city.

According to tradition Barcelona was founded by Phoenician or Carthaginian settlers, and some historians credit the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca with naming it Barcino in the 3rd century BCE, though this theory has been questioned. Coins of the 3rd century BCE found at the foot of Montjuïc carry the name Barkeno in Iberian script.

In the Middle Ages Barcelona became the capital of the County of Barcelona. After the union with Aragon it remained capital of the Principality of Catalonia and the most important city of the Crown of Aragon, until Valencia overtook it shortly before 1516. Its industrial rise began in 1833, when Catalonia's textile industry began to use steam power. It became capital of autonomous Catalonia in 1931 and was taken by the fascists in 1939.

Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia and the second most populous municipality of Spain. Its old centre, the Barri Gòtic, has buildings from medieval times and some from the Roman settlement. Works of Antoni Gaudí and Lluís Domènech i Montaner are World Heritage Sites, and the city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics.
bareilly: Bareilly lies in the Indo-Gangetic Plains on the bank of the Ramganga River, about 252 kilometres north-west of Lucknow and 265 kilometres east of New Delhi. The plain is level and well watered, with fertile alluvial soil, although the lower plain is flood-prone. According to the Mahabharata, the region, called Panchala, was the birthplace of Draupadi, and folklore says that Gautama Buddha visited the ancient fortress city of Ahichchhatra.

The earliest settlement was founded in 1537 by the Rajput chieftain Jagat Singh Katehriya, who named it after his two sons Bansaldev and Baraldev. The town came under Mughal rule in 1569, and in 1657 the Mughal governor Mukrand Rai laid the foundation of the modern city. As Mughal power weakened, the Kingdom of Rohilkhand rose, with Bareilly as a major centre. Under Hafiz Rahmat Khan Barech, Rohilkhand blocked Maratha expansion into northern India at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

In 1774 the combined forces of Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the East India Company defeated Hafiz Rahmat Khan, who was killed in battle, ending Rohilla rule. The Nawab of Awadh surrendered Rohilkhand to the Company in a treaty of 10 November 1801. A military station was established south of the city in 1811, and a fort was built in 1816. Bareilly was freed by rebels during the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and remained independent under Khan Bahadur Khan until the British re-annexed it in 1858.

Bareilly is a city in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh and the centre of the historical region of Rohilkhand. It is the place of origin of the Barelvi movement, a Sunni Islamic movement formed by the scholar Ahmad Raza Khan to counter the growing influence of the Deobandi movement; his shrine at the Bareilly Dargah is visited by millions of followers each year. The city has been known as Nath Nagri because of its ancient Shiva temples, and is a centre of furniture manufacturing and of trade in cotton, cereal and sugar.
barometer: On 27 July 1630 Giovanni Battista Baliani wrote to Galileo Galilei about a siphon led over a hill about 21 m high that failed to work: the water in the limb sank to about 10 m above the reservoir. Galileo answered that the power of a vacuum held the water up until its weight grew too great, a restatement of the old doctrine that nature abhors a vacuum. After his Discorsi reached Rome in December 1638, Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti sought a better way to produce a vacuum. W. E. Knowles Middleton places their experiment between 1639 and 1643, with Athanasius Kircher and Niccolò Zucchi present.

Torricelli, who had been Galileo's amanuensis in the last three months of his life, read the results differently. In a letter to Michelangelo Ricci in 1644 he argued that the weight of the atmosphere explained the resistance, and that it was foolish to attribute to a vacuum what followed from another evident cause.

Marin Mersenne was shown the experiment by Torricelli toward the end of 1644, and in 1646 Blaise Pascal and Pierre Petit repeated and perfected it. Pascal tested the Aristotelian claim that vapours from the liquid filled the space above it by comparing water with wine, thought more spiritous. He did so in public, inviting the Aristotelians to predict the result. They expected the wine to stand lower, and it did not.

Mercury barometers broke at sea, and in 1668 Robert Hooke's marine barometer, made by Henry Hunt, was presented to the Royal Society. The compact sympiesometer was widely used on ships in the early 19th century. Leibniz proposed an aneroid barometer around 1700, and Lucien Vidi invented a working one in 1844.

Pressure readings and the pressure tendency, the change over time, have been used in weather forecasting since the late 19th century. Combined with wind observations they allow reasonably accurate short-term forecasts, and readings from a network of stations produced maps of air pressure, the first form of the modern weather map. A rapid fall suggests an approaching low-pressure system and more chance of rain, while a rapid rise follows a cold front and goes with clearing skies. Readings are corrected for temperature, since the density of mercury changes, and reduced to sea level.
bartolome-de-las-casas: Bartolomé de las Casas was born in Seville on 11 November 1484. For centuries his birth was dated to 1474, until archival work in the 1970s uncovered records of a contemporary lawsuit showing that he was born a decade later. His father, Pedro de las Casas, was a merchant. He arrived in Hispaniola as one of the first Spanish settlers and took part in the colonial economy built on forced Indigenous labour. In 1513, as a chaplain, he joined the conquest of Cuba, where he witnessed many atrocities against the Ciboney and Guanahatabey. He later wrote that he saw cruelty on a scale no living being has ever seen.

In 1515 he gave up his Indigenous laborers and his encomienda and met King Ferdinand to argue against the encomienda system. He was given the title Protector of the Indians. In his early writings he advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labour, a position he later retracted, writing that black slavery was as unjust as Indian slavery. His attempt at peaceful settlement in Venezuela failed, and in 1522 he entered the Dominican monastery of Santa Cruz in Santo Domingo, taking vows in 1523.

He worked as a missionary among the Maya of Guatemala and lobbied for the abolition of the encomienda, winning an important victory in the New Laws of 1542. He was consecrated Bishop of Chiapas on 30 March 1544. Conflicts with the encomenderos and colonists forced him back to Spain. In 1550 he took part in the Valladolid debate, in which Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that the Indians were less than human. De Las Casas maintained that they were fully human and that forcible subjugation was unjustifiable.

De Las Casas resigned his bishopric and spent the rest of his life at the imperial court, where he had great influence on matters concerning the Indies. He died on 18 July 1566. A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written in 1542 and published at Seville in 1552, was one of the first attempts by a colonial-era Spanish writer to describe the mistreatment of Indigenous peoples. His efforts improved the legal status of Indigenous people and sharpened the ethical debate over colonialism, though he did not change Spanish policy as a whole. After his death he was widely venerated, and a cause for beatification was opened.
bartolome-esteban-murillo: Murillo was probably born in December 1617 to Gaspar Esteban, a barber surgeon, and María Pérez Murillo, and was baptised in the parish of Santa María Magdalena in Seville on 1 January 1618. After his parents died in 1627 and 1628 he became the ward of his older sister Ana and her husband Juan Agustín Lagares, and he stayed in their house until his marriage in 1645.

He studied in Seville in the workshop of Juan del Castillo, his uncle and godfather. His first works were also influenced by Francisco de Zurbarán, Jusepe de Ribera and Alonso Cano. According to the painter and art historian Antonio Palomino he travelled to Madrid in 1642, but there is little evidence for this, and Palomino denied claims by Joachim von Sandrart that he went to Italy.

In 1645 Murillo married Beatriz Cabrera y Villalobos, with whom he had ten children. The year of his marriage he received his first major commission, eleven canvases for the convent of San Francisco in Seville, on which he worked until 1648. They show a range from the tenebrism of the Ecstasy of St Francis to the softly luminous style, seen in the Death of St Clare, that became typical of his mature work. Also about 1645 he painted The Young Beggar, now in the Louvre, the first of his many paintings of children, in which the influence of Velázquez is apparent.

After a pair of pictures for Seville Cathedral he specialised in the Virgin and Child and the Immaculate Conception. He was again in Madrid from 1658 to 1660. On returning to Seville he was one of the founders of the Academia de Bellas Artes, sharing its direction in 1660 with the architect Francisco Herrera the Younger. This was his period of most activity, and the paintings for Santa María la Blanca were completed in 1665.

Murillo died in Seville on 3 April 1682, a few months after he fell from a scaffold while working on a fresco at the church of the Capuchines in Cádiz. He had many pupils and followers, and the imitation of his paintings ensured his reputation in Spain and his fame throughout Europe. Before the 19th century his work was more widely known than that of any other Spanish artist, and Gainsborough and Greuze were among those influenced by his style. His paintings of flower girls, street urchins and beggars form an extensive record of the everyday life of his times.
bartolomeu-dias: Dias came from a family with a maritime background. One of his ancestors, Dinis Dias e Fernandes, explored the African coast in the 1440s. Tracing his own biography is complicated by the existence of several Portuguese seafarers of the same name. In 1481 he accompanied an expedition led by Diogo de Azambuja to build the fortress and trading post of São Jorge da Mina in the Gulf of Guinea, and indirect evidence suggests he may have joined Diogo Cão's first expedition to the Congo River. On 10 October 1486 King John II of Portugal granted him an annuity of 6,000 reis for services to come.

Probably in July or August 1487 Dias left Lisbon with three ships, to continue the exploration advanced by Cão and to look for Prester John, a Christian ruler believed to reign somewhere beyond Europe. He carried stone pillars, padrões, to mark landfalls, and six Africans kidnapped by Cão and taught Portuguese, whom he meant to leave along the coast. On 8 December 1487 he reached modern Walvis Bay. The ships then turned southwest, away from land; historians debate whether a storm drove them or they sought better winds. After 30 days at sea, on 4 February 1488, they reached the southern cape of Africa at what became Mossel Bay.

They continued east until 12 March 1488, when they anchored at Kwaaihoek. The crew were restless and the ships battered, and the officers unanimously urged a return, which Dias accepted. In May 1488 he first saw the Cape of Good Hope; tradition says he named it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it. He reached Lisbon in December 1488 after 16 months. Almost all maritime records were destroyed in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, and much comes from João de Barros, writing about sixty years later. His reception at court was muted.

Dias contributed to the design and construction of the São Gabriel and São Rafael used by Vasco da Gama, and accompanied da Gama's fleet to the Cape Verde Islands in 1497. In 1500 he was a captain on Pedro Álvares Cabral's expedition, which reached Brazil on 22 April 1500. He died on 29 May 1500 when four ships, his among them, were lost in a storm off the Cape of Good Hope. His grandson Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Luanda in 1576.
bas-rhin: Bas-Rhin, meaning Lower Rhine, is a department of Alsace in the Grand Est region of France. The name refers to its lower altitude, since it lies downstream of Haut-Rhin. The Rhine forms its eastern border, and the area includes foothills of the Vosges Mountains. To the north lies the Palatinate Forest in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and to the east the state of Baden-Württemberg. Strasbourg is its prefecture and most populous commune. With Haut-Rhin it formed the traditional region of Alsace, which until 1871 also included the area now called the Territoire de Belfort. It is the last French department to keep the term Bas in its name.

Bas-Rhin is one of the original 83 departments, created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution. On 14 January 1790 the National Constituent Assembly decreed that Alsace be divided into two departments with Strasbourg and Colmar as their capitals. Its borders then changed many times. In 1793 it absorbed newly annexed territories such as the County of Sarrewerden and the County of Drulingen. In 1808 some territories east of the Rhine, including the city of Kehl, were annexed, and in 1814 and 1815 the treaties of Paris first gave France the lands north of the Lauter, including Landau, and then took them away. Troops from Baden and Saxony occupied the department from June 1815 to November 1818.

In 1871 the Treaty of Frankfurt annexed it to Germany, and it became the Bezirk Unterelsass in the Reichsland Elsaß-Lothringen. It became French again in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles and kept the cantons of Schirmeck and Saales that Germany had taken from the Vosges. The Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp operated there between 1941 and 1944. Kehl was attached to Bas-Rhin in 1944 and reassigned to West Germany in 1953. In 1982 the department joined the newly created Alsace region.

Strasbourg is the official seat of the European Parliament and of the Council of Europe. The department had 1,163,810 inhabitants in 2023 and is densely populated, with more than twice the French average density. The Rhine has always been of great historical and economic importance to the area. On 1 January 2021 the departmental councils of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin merged into the European Collectivity of Alsace. Its inhabitants are known as Bas-Rhinois.
basel-landschaft: Basel-Landschaft, also called Basel-Country, and informally Baselland or Baselbiet, is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation. It is composed of five districts, with Liestal as its capital, and is traditionally considered a half-canton, the other half being Basel-Stadt. It lies essentially south of the Rhine and north of the Jura Mountains, in the northwestern corner of Switzerland, and borders Basel-Stadt, Aargau, Solothurn and Jura, with international borders with France and Germany. The Ergolz and the Birs drain its lands. Its shape is very irregular, and its borders cut across several towns.

In Roman times the area was a centre of Roman activity. The remains of Augusta Raurica, in what is now Augst, show a city of about 20,000 people around 200 CE, and the site includes the best-preserved amphitheatre north of the Alps. With Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft formed the historic canton of Basel, which joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. Until the end of the 16th century most of its land belonged to the city of Basel, on which the countryside was economically dependent, and the castles and residences of Basel merchants dominated much of the landscape. After Napoleon's visit in 1798 the country achieved equality with the city.

After 1830 political quarrels and armed conflict broke out in the canton, partly over the rights of the rural population. They culminated in the uprising of 1833, including the Battle of the Hülftenschanz near Frenkendorf, and led to the separation of Basel-Landschaft from the city on 26 August 1833.

A movement for reunification gained momentum after 1900, when many parts of Basel-Landschaft became industrialised. The two half cantons agreed in principle to merge, but in 1969 the people of Basel-Landschaft voted down the proposal, perhaps because the economic gap between the two had closed. Since then they have signed agreements to co-operate, such as the canton's contribution to the University of Basel since 1976. In 1988 the canton wrote into its constitution the aim of recognition of the two Basels as full cantons. The population is predominantly German-speaking.
basel-stadt: Basel-Stadt, or Basel-City, is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation, composed of three municipalities, Basel, Riehen and Bettingen, with Basel as its capital. It is traditionally a half-canton, the other half being Basel-Landschaft. It is the smallest canton by area, just 37 square kilometres, and one of the northernmost and lowest, lying on both sides of the Rhine. Basel stands at the Rhine knee, where the river turns from a westerly to a northerly flow, marking the change from the High Rhine to the Upper Rhine. The territories of Switzerland, France and Germany meet in the middle of the Rhine, about 150 metres north of the Dreiländereck monument.

Together with Basel-Landschaft, Basel-Stadt was part of the Canton of Basel, which joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. After political quarrels and armed conflict, partly over the rights of the population of the agricultural areas, the canton was divided and Basel-Landschaft separated from the city on 26 August 1833. A movement for reunification gained momentum after 1900, when many parts of Basel-Landschaft became industrialised, but the people of Basel-Landschaft voted against reunion in 1969 and again in September 2014.

The present constitution of the canton dates from 1889. In 1966 Basel-Stadt became the first German-speaking canton to allow women to vote, five years before the right was extended to all Swiss women in 1971.

The chemical and pharmaceutical industries are the most significant industries in the canton, and Basel is the worldwide seat of the Bank for International Settlements. The port on the Rhine offers landlocked Switzerland its only direct connection to the sea, and the airport of Basel-Mulhouse lies 4 kilometres inside French territory. The Carnival of Basel, whose central tradition, the Morgestraich, begins at 4 a.m. and is followed by 72 hours of festivities, and the Autumn Fair, the biggest in Switzerland, are major events. The canton is known for two biscuits, the Basler Läckerli and the Basler Brunsli.
bashkirs: The Bashkirs, or Bashkorts, are a Turkic people indigenous to Russia, concentrated in Bashkortostan and the historical region on both sides of the Ural Mountains. The Bashkir group was formed by Turkic tribes of South Siberian and Central Asian origin who wandered for a long time in the Aral-Syr Darya steppes, before migrating to the southern Urals between the end of the 9th century and the beginning of the 10th. The name Bashqurt has been known since the 10th century. Most researchers read it as bash, head or leader, plus qurt, wolf, and a legend tells how a wolf guided the first seven Bashkir tribes from the Syr Darya valley to their land.

The first Arabic and Persian reports of the Bashkirs date from the 9th century, including the account of Sallam al-Tardjuman, who travelled to their territory around 850. In the early 10th century Ahmad ibn Fadlan, an envoy of the Baghdad caliph to Volga Bulgaria, wrote the first ethnographic description, calling them a warlike and powerful people who bred cattle and worshipped twelve gods. By 1226 Genghis Khan had incorporated their lands into his empire, and in the 13th and 14th centuries Bashkortostan was part of the Golden Horde. Afterwards the Bashkirs were divided among the Nogai Horde, the Khanate of Kazan and the Khanate of Sibir.

From the middle of the 16th century the Tsardom of Russia gradually conquered the Bashkirs. They took part in uprisings in 1662–64, 1681–84 and 1704–11, and in 1676 a rebellion under Seyid Sadir gave the Russian army great difficulties. The founding of Orenburg in 1735 brought a fourth insurrection that lasted six years.

In the late 1780s they gained tax-free status in exchange for providing soldiers to the Tsarist army, and in 1798 Russia formed an irregular Bashkir army. On 15 November 1917 the Bashkir Regional Shuro proclaimed the first independent Bashkir Republic, and in March 1919 the Bashkir Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was formed.

The Bashkirs traditionally practised agriculture, cattle-rearing and bee-keeping, and the half-nomadic among them herded cattle through the mountains or the steppes. Before Islam they practised animism and shamanism and incorporated Tengrism; they began converting in the 10th century, and Islam was finally established among them in the 1320s and 1330s. Most are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school. Their oral tradition includes the epic poem Ural Batyr, which tells how the hero Ural gives up eternal life and from his body emerge the Ural Mountains. In the 2021 Russian census 1,571,879 ethnic Bashkirs were recorded in Russia.
basil-ii: Basil II was born in 958, a porphyrogennetos, born into the purple, as were his father Romanos II and his grandfather Constantine VII. His mother Theophano was the daughter of a poor tavern-keeper named Krateros. Romanos crowned him co-emperor on 22 April 960 and died on 15 March 963 at the age of 24, a death commonly thought at the time to have been poisoning with hemlock. Nikephoros II and John I then ruled, brilliant commanders but poor administrators. Basil II became sole emperor in 976, and spent his early years learning administration and military science while Basil Lekapenos hoped to use him as a puppet.

The early years were dominated by civil wars against two Anatolian generals, Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas, which ended shortly after Phokas died and Skleros submitted in 989. He sent his sister Anna Porphyrogenita to Vladimir I of Kiev in return for military support, forming the Varangian Guard, and the marriage led to the Christianization of the Kievan Rus. After fighting in Syria against the Fatimids, Basil rode through Asia Minor to Aleppo in sixteen days, arriving in April 995, and the Fatimid commander withdrew without battle.

Against Bulgaria he suffered a serious defeat at the Battle of the Gates of Trajan in 986 after besieging Sofia with 30,000 men. Samuel of Bulgaria became his main adversary, and Basil eventually brought the First Bulgarian Empire under complete subjugation after a long struggle. In 1001 he inherited the territories of the Georgian prince David III of Tao, organised as the theme of Iberia, and in 1021 Seneqerim-John of Vaspurakan ceded his kingdom in exchange for estates in Sebasteia.

Basil campaigned with his army rather than sending orders from Constantinople, ate the same rations as his soldiers, and took the children of dead officers under his protection. His laws protected small landowners and lowered their taxes, and he reduced the power of the great landowning families and filled the treasury. He left the empire at its largest territorial extent in four centuries. His successors were largely incompetent, but the empire flourished for decades after his death. Basil is seen as a Greek national hero but is a despised figure among Bulgarians.
basques: The Basques are a Southwestern European ethnic group, characterised by the Basque language, a common culture and shared genetic ancestry with the ancient Vascones and Aquitanians, and are considered among the last remaining direct descendants of Neolithic European populations in Europe. The English word Basque comes from French, itself from Gascon Basco, cognate with Spanish Vasco and ultimately from Latin Vasco, plural Vascones. Because the language predates the Indo-European languages and blood groups and other classical markers are distinctive, a long-held popular view made the Basques living fossils of the earliest modern humans in Europe. Yet although genetically distinctive in some ways owing to isolation, they are typically European in their Y-DNA and mtDNA sequences, which are widespread across the western half of the continent.

Strabo and Pliny mentioned Basque tribes in Roman times, among them the Vascones and the Aquitani, and there is enough evidence to support the hypothesis that they spoke old varieties of the Basque language, known as Aquitanian. In the early Middle Ages the territory between the Ebro and Garonne rivers was known as Vasconia, a vaguely defined ethnic area and political entity struggling to fend off pressure from the Visigothic kingdom and Arab rule to the south and the Frankish push from the north.

By the turn of the first millennium Vasconia had fragmented into feudal regions such as Soule and Labourd. South of the Pyrenees, Castile, Pamplona and the Pyrenean counties of Aragon, Sobrarbe, Ribagorça and Pallars emerged in the 9th and 10th centuries as the main regional entities with a Basque population.

The Basque Country, Euskal Herria in Basque, lies around the western end of the Pyrenees on the Bay of Biscay and is divided into at least three administrative units: the Basque Autonomous Community, made up of Álava, Biscay and Gipuzkoa, and Navarre in Spain, and the Basque Country Agglomeration Community in the French Basque Country. The Basque Autonomous Community has 2,123,000 inhabitants, and its largest cities are Bilbao, San Sebastián and Vitoria-Gasteiz.

The identifying language is Basque, or Euskara, spoken by 25 to 30 per cent of the region's population. Basques call themselves euskaldun, Basque speaker, and their country Euskal Herria, country of the Basque language. Knowledge of the language declined for many years under Franco's dictatorship owing to official persecution. Basques have a close attachment to the home, etxea, especially the traditional self-sufficient family-run farm, the baserri, and many surnames come from farm names, such as Etxeberria, the new house. Gastronomical societies, txoko, are food clubs where men gather to cook. Large numbers have emigrated, often as shepherds, ranchers, fishers and merchants, and Basque descendants live in North America, Latin America, South Africa and Australia.
basra: Basra lies on the banks of the Shatt al-Arab, which empties into the Persian Gulf, near the border with Iran. Its Arabic name, al-Basrah, means the overwatcher, perhaps an allusion to its origin as an Arab military base; others derive it from the Aramaic basratha, a place of huts or settlement. It was built in 636 as a camp for the Arab tribesmen of the armies of the Rashidun caliph Umar. The original site, about 15 km south-west of the modern city, is marked by the Imam Ali Mosque, and Basra is home to the first mosque built outside the Arabian Peninsula.

Under the Abbasids, who took Basra in the late 740s, it became an intellectual centre and home to the Basra School of Grammar, rival and sister of the school of Kufa. Its notable figures include the polymath Ibn al-Haytham, the writer al-Jahiz and the Sufi mystic Rabia Basri. The city was a centre of the slave trade in Mesopotamia until the Zanj rebellion of agricultural slaves, whose forces sacked it in 871. The Qarmatians invaded and devastated it in 923.

After the Mongols under Hulegu Khan sacked Baghdad in 1258, Basra by some accounts capitulated to avoid a massacre. Ibn Battuta visited in the 14th century. Portugal controlled the city from 1526, and the Ottoman Empire captured it in 1668. It was under Safavid control from 1697 to 1701, and the Zand dynasty under Karim Khan Zand occupied it briefly after a long siege. In 1884 the Ottomans created the vilayet of Basra. British forces captured the city in 1914, and it passed to Mandatory Iraq and then to the Kingdom of Iraq, independent in 1932.

Basra is the capital of Basra Governorate and the third largest city in Iraq, after Baghdad and Mosul. Its position on the Gulf makes it a major port, and it is the country's only coastal region, along with its adjoining governorate. During World War II it was an important port through which much equipment sent to the Soviet Union flowed. The University of Basrah was founded in 1964. The population is mostly Arab Shia Muslims, with a large Sunni minority.
basse-terre: Basse-Terre stands at the south-western corner of the island of Basse-Terre, the western half of Guadeloupe, about 100 km north of Dominica. The town grew on a narrow coastal strip between the Caribbean Sea and the first hills of the ridge that divides the island, with the volcanic massif of the Soufrière to the north-east. The name comes from the seamen's vocabulary of the 17th century, which called a land or coast sheltered from the wind a basse-terre.

The site of the present cathedral was first a village of American Indian horticulturists and potters. French settlement began in 1635, when Charles Liénard de l'Olive and Jean du Plessis d'Ossonville landed with 4 missionaries and 550 colonists at Pointe Allègre, and relations with the Native Americans soon turned to war. Charles Houël du Petit Pré moved to the right bank of the Galion and built a fort, a church followed, and the town was organised around the chapel and the fort. English privateers burned it in 1691 and 1703.

A British force captured the island on 23 January 1759, and France recovered it in 1763. Pointe-à-Pitre was founded in 1764 in a better position to receive the ocean swell. In 1794 Victor Hugues recaptured Guadeloupe from the British and abolished slavery. In 1802 General Antoine Richepanse, sent by Napoleon to restore slavery, fought Louis Delgrès, who retreated to the fort on 20 May and left it on 22 May. After the cyclone of September 1928 the architect Ali Tur built the courthouse and a market. In 1976, because of the Soufrière's activity, 73,600 inhabitants of Guadeloupe were evacuated.

Basse-Terre is the prefecture of Guadeloupe, though Pointe-à-Pitre is the larger city, and holds the courts, including the Court of Appeal, and the seat of the diocese. Fort Delgrès, begun by Houël as Fort Saint-Charles and renamed in 1989, is a classified historical monument, as is the Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, which marked the town's foundation. The Bologne distillery, producing rum, remains its main local industry.
basses-pyrenees: Pyrénées-Atlantiques, named after the Pyrenees mountain range and the Atlantic Ocean, lies in the south-west corner of metropolitan France, in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine. It covers the French Basque Country and the Béarn, and its prefecture is Pau. It is bordered by the departments of Landes, Hautes-Pyrénées and Gers, by the Bay of Biscay to the west and by the Spanish provinces of Huesca, Navarre and Gipuzkoa to the south. The Pyrenees cross it from east to west, and the border with Spain follows the chain. Its highest point is the Pic Palas, in the Balaïtous massif, at 2,974 m.

Originally named Basses-Pyrénées, it was one of the 83 departments created during the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790. It comprised Labourd and Soule, in the provinces of Guyenne and Gascony, as well as Lower Navarre, still at least nominally part of the Kingdom of Navarre, and the Béarn. Six districts were set up, with the prefecture first at Navarrenx before it moved to Pau on 14 October 1790.

The reform ended native institutions and laws. All the Basque estates representatives from Labourd opposed the new layout, the representatives of Lower Navarre refused to vote in Paris on the ground that they were not part of the Kingdom of France, and those of Soule voted against. The brothers Garat, representing Labourd, voted yes, thinking it would give them a say in later decisions. In 1800 the six districts were replaced by five arrondissements: Pau, Orthez, Bayonne, Mauléon and Oloron. In 1926 a reform under the government of Raymond Poincaré abolished those of Orthez and Mauléon, leaving the three that remain.

In the 1950s the department formed part of the newly created region of Aquitaine. In 1969 it was renamed Pyrénées-Atlantiques, because its inhabitants found Basses-Pyrénées pejorative compared with the name of the Hautes-Pyrénées.

The west is mainly inhabited by the Basques and the east by the Béarnais, who have shared a department since the Revolution; from 1790 to 1969 the inhabitants were called Bas-Pyrénéens. Gascon, a dialect of Occitan, and Basque, a language isolate, are indigenous in their districts, but French is the predominant native language. Pau and the urban area of Bayonne, Anglet and Biarritz are the two main urban concentrations. The department has 706,564 inhabitants in 2023 and is known for its tourism and its links with Spain. Its coat of arms combines those of Lower Navarre, Béarn, Labourd and Soule.
bastia: Bastia lies in the north-east of Corsica at the base of the Cap Corse, between the sea and the mountain. The city is 35 km from the northern tip of the Cap Corse, 50 km west of the Italian island of Elba and 90 km from continental Italy, which can be seen on a few days a year when visibility is excellent. The climate is Mediterranean, with an average annual temperature of 16.3 °C and about 240 sunny days a year.

In Roman times the north-eastern part of the present commune formed a pieve, the oldest known administrative division, occupied by the Vanacimi people. Bastia did not exist: Ptolemy, Strabo and Pliny do not mention it. At the end of the 9th century the pieve of Mantino depended on the Loretesi lords, driven out in 1072 by the Da Furiani with the help of the Marquis of Massa. Before the Genoese came, the pieve of Orto held several small communities, and on the coast stood a fishing hamlet called Porto Cardo.

The Genoese soon felt the need to protect Bastia from attack by sea and began to build a bastiglia and a citadel in the time of the governor Leonello Lomellini. The settlement grew, prospered and became more important than Cardo, and it was the capital during Genoese rule. The sea and the mountains decided where houses stood, and the town spread later onto the slopes, drawn toward the water at the Place Saint-Nicolas.

Bastia is a commune of Haute-Corse and the department's capital, with the second-highest population of any commune on the island after Ajaccio. It is the island's principal port and commercial town. The Old Port, in a narrow cove that gives good protection from the weather, was at the heart of the first development. The centre consists mainly of the citadel, also called Terra Nova, the Palace of the Governors, the Old Port and the market place, and the buildings along the Paoli Boulevard. The Church of Sainte-Marie, a former cathedral built in 1495 and heavily remodelled in the early 17th century, stands in the citadel.
batavian-republic: After the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the Patriot party revolted against Stadtholder William V but was struck down in September 1787 when Frederick William II of Prussia intervened. Most Patriots went into exile in France, and the Dutch Republic became in effect an Anglo-Prussian protectorate, formalised by the Act of Guarantee in 1788. The French Revolution embraced many Patriot ideas, and the Patriots hoped to be treated as a sister republic rather than conquered territory. In the severe winter of 1794 and 1795 a French army under General Charles Pichegru, with a Dutch contingent under General Herman Willem Daendels, crossed the frozen rivers. Many cities rose before the French arrived, and William fled to England on 18 January 1795.

The republic was proclaimed on 19 January 1795. The harsh Treaty of The Hague of 16 May 1795 imposed territorial concessions, a large indemnity and a French army of occupation of 25,000 men, and it made the state a French client, the first of the sister republics. Even so, the programme of reform was driven mostly by Dutch needs. A National Assembly met at The Hague on 1 March 1796, divided between unitary democrats such as Pieter Vreede and federalists such as Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck.

The constitution of 1798 was the first in Dutch history of a democratic character. France supported coups in turn: Daendels seized the Assembly on 12 June 1798 and arrested its members, and a coup in 1801 brought a new regime and a revised constitution.

From October 1801 the state was called the Batavian Commonwealth. Napoleon disliked the Dutch government, partly because Amsterdam bankers had refused him a large loan in 1800. After a clash over French customs men in November 1804 he settled on a new constitution, and Schimmelpenninck became Grand Pensionary. This regime also failed to satisfy him. The republic ended on 5 June 1806 with the accession of his brother, Louis Bonaparte, as king of Holland.

The Kingdom of Holland lasted four years: Louis refused to follow French dictates, abdicated on 2 July 1810 and the territory was incorporated into the French Empire. After the French defeat the independent Netherlands re-emerged in 1813, and William VI of Orange landed at Scheveningen on 30 November. The republic's reforms outlasted it. The confederal structure of the old Dutch Republic was replaced for good by a unitary state, a type of ministerial government appeared for the first time, and many present government departments date their history to this period. Its influence also eased the move to the more democratic constitutional revision of 1848 by Johan Rudolph Thorbecke.
battambang: Battambang lies on the Sangkae River, which winds through the province of the same name. The province is considered the rice bowl of Cambodia, and the city has many mills that process rice for national and international markets; its jasmine rice is well known. The river long served as the main link to Phnom Penh and Saigon, and the city is also joined to Phnom Penh and Bangkok by National Highway 5.

Battambang began as a fishing village on the Sangkae River in the 11th century, founded under the Khmer Empire. In 1795 Siam annexed much of north-western Cambodia as the province of Inner Cambodia and ruled Battambang as a provincial capital through the Abhaiwongse family. By 1880 it was an important trading city of about 2,500 residents. The Siamese built one road, a fort for the governor, a market, several pagodas and a Catholic hospital.

In 1907 the province was ceded to France and rejoined Cambodia within French Indochina. The French laid out a grid of streets, canals and bridges in what is now the Heritage Conservation Area, linked both riverbanks by two bridges in 1917 and in 1926 began a second phase of building, with a railway to Phnom Penh, villas, the central market and state buildings.

In 1953 Prince Norodom Sihanouk chose Battambang as the centre of Cambodia's independence movement. It was Cambodia's second largest city in the 20th century, with garment factories, an airport, schools and a university. Under Democratic Kampuchea its population was forcibly evacuated into labour camps and land tenure was abolished; the Battambang Provincial Museum became a prison, and the Phnom Sampeau killing caves, a Khmer Rouge execution site, lie about six kilometres from the city. A Vietnamese invasion toppled the Khmer Rouge in 1980, but the province remained a Khmer Rouge stronghold into the 1990s. Guerrillas besieged the city in 1990 without taking it, and conflict around it continued until 1997.

Battambang is the capital of its province and one of Cambodia's larger cities. The municipality established a Heritage Protection Area in 2009 to safeguard around 800 historic buildings, among them French colonial architecture and the Art Deco central market, Psar Nath, built in 1936. Wat Damrei Sar, built in the 19th century, is the oldest pagoda in the city. UNESCO named it a City of Gastronomy in 2023, the first Cambodian city in its Creative Cities Network.
battle-of-albulena: Skanderbeg had fought the Ottoman Empire since 1444, and after more than a decade of war his resources were worn out. His siege of Berat in 1455 ended in catastrophe when an Ottoman counterattack fell on the Albanians during his temporary absence. Afterwards some of his most trusted officers deserted. Moisi Golemi returned in May 1456 at the head of an Ottoman force, was defeated at the Battle of Oranik and was taken back without punishment.

A graver loss was his nephew Hamza Kastrioti, one of his most important officers, who had grown dissatisfied with Skanderbeg's increasing power and was promised control of much of Albania once it was conquered. Relations with Venice were at their lowest point. Alfonso V of Aragon and Pope Calixtus III, his allies, could not provide for him fully, and a fleet the pope promised in 1457 did not arrive.

By the end of May 1457 an Ottoman army of between 50,000 and 80,000 men approached, against which Skanderbeg had between 8,000 and 10,000. He stalled the akıncı vanguard marching through Dibër, then withdrew before the main force. Since both Ottoman commanders knew his usual ambushes, he split his army into several groups and ordered them to march through the forests and mountains in different directions, supplied by the local people and by depots, and not to assemble or attack without his word.

The Ottomans pillaged the Mat valley and camped at Albulena, north of Mount Tumenishta and south of modern Laç. Through July and August Skanderbeg stayed out of sight, and rumours spread that he had fled. On 2 September his reassembled army attacked the camp in three groups with a great noise of clashing metal. The Ottomans, believing the attackers more numerous than they were, panicked. Their dead may have been as many as 30,000, though it is unlikely that more than 15,000 were killed; 15,000 were taken prisoner and twenty-four standards were captured.

Hamza Kastrioti was captured and sent as a prisoner to Naples. An Ottoman envoy came to ransom the standard bearers and forty distinguished prisoners and proposed a truce, which Skanderbeg would accept only if Svetigrad and Berat were restored to him. In 1460 Sultan Mehmed II and Skanderbeg signed an armistice that lasted three years, giving Skanderbeg the opportunity to cross to Italy and help Ferdinand I of Naples. The historian Franz Babinger called the battle Skanderbeg's most brilliant victory. Desertions from his army became rare afterwards, but the war continued until the fall of Krujë in 1478.
battle-of-bir-hakeim: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.
battle-of-koppam: From his accession Rajadhiraja Chola I sought to subdue the Chalukyas, who ruled parts of northern Karnataka and the south of present-day Maharashtra, and to add their lands to the Chola Empire. His first invasion, in 1047–48, had failed. On the second expedition he led a large army north and plundered the province of Rattamandalam, with his brother and heir-apparent Rajendra Chola II following in the rear.

According to the Chola sources and the Thiruvalandur copper plate, Rajadhiraja had personally led the attack on Kalyanapura, also called Kalyani, the modern Basavakalyan. Someshvara I fled when the city was attacked, returned with an army and was beaten again, and the Chola king then withdrew towards Kollapura. The copper plate says that Someshvara gathered a huge army and called out for battle as the Chola withdrew, and that the Chola turned to meet him at the place called Koppam.

The copper plate describes columns of foot soldiers, horses and elephants engaging their counterparts, with Rajadhiraja fighting from his elephant until a downpour of Chalukya arrows killed him. The Chola troops, who had been holding the upper hand, panicked and began to retreat. Rajendra II, commanding the reserve, took over the army, rallied it and inflicted heavy losses, forcing Someshvara to flee. Chola sources record that the elephants, horses and camels of the Chalukyas, a large booty and the queens of Someshvara fell into Chola hands. Rajendra is reported to have set up a victory pillar at Kolhapur before returning to his country.

The battle is known chiefly from the Chola side: an inscription dated to 1054 and Rajendra Chola II's Manimangalam record of 1055. The latter gives the victory to Rajendra and says that Ahavamalla, as it calls the Chalukya king, became afraid, incurred disgrace and ran away. The year is given as 1054, or as 1052 by the historian Sen. The site is also uncertain. The Manimangalam inscription places Koppam on the bank of the great river; the scholar Fleet identified it with Khidrapur, 30 miles south-east of Kolhapur, taking the river to be the Krishna, while other historians have put it near Maski.
bavaria: Bavaria is a landlocked state of Germany. It borders Baden-Württemberg, Hesse, Thuringia and Saxony within Germany, and Switzerland across Lake Constance, Austria to the south and the Czech Republic to the east. Two major rivers, the Danube and the Main, flow through it, and the Bavarian Forest and the Bohemian Forest form most of the frontier with the Czech Republic. Its modern borders take in Altbayern and parts of the historical regions of Franconia and Swabia, and it is divided into seven administrative regions: Upper Palatinate, Upper Bavaria and Lower Bavaria in Altbayern, Upper, Middle and Lower Franconia, and Swabia.

Humans have lived in Bavaria since the Paleolithic era, and Celtic tribes of the Bronze Age, such as the Boii, were the first documented inhabitants of the Bavarian Alps. Archaeologists know of a large Celtic Iron Age settlement at Feldmoching-Hasenbergl, north of Munich, where up to 500 people lived from 450 BCE. At Manching in Upper Bavaria an unfortified, semi-urban society prospered from the 3rd century BCE until the early 1st century CE, with food ovens, pottery kilns and metallurgical furnaces. By 200 BCE it was trading, and finds of coins and a golden tree suggest contact with distant Italo-Greek communities.

In the first century CE the Roman Empire incorporated the territory into the provinces of Raetia and Noricum. After the empire collapsed, the Duchy of Bavaria was created in Francia in 555 CE. It later became part of East Francia and controlled land in modern Austria, Slovenia and Italy. Within the Holy Roman Empire Bavaria gained elector status in 1623, during the Thirty Years' War, and it became the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. After the unification of Germany it stayed a kingdom within the German Empire until the end of the First World War. The modern state was established in 1945 and became part of West Germany in 1949.

The capital and largest city is Munich; other major cities are Nuremberg, Augsburg, Regensburg and Ingolstadt. With an area of 70,550 square kilometres it is the largest German state, and it has about 13 million inhabitants. The official name is the Free State of Bavaria. Its culture is strongly shaped by its Catholic heritage, and the Bavarian language, a group of German dialects spoken in Bavaria and Austria by around 12 million people, is the largest German dialect. It has two official flags of equal status, one striped white and blue and one with white and blue lozenges.
beijing: Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of the municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. The highest point of the municipality is Mount Dongling, at 2,303 metres, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The name Beijing means 'Northern Capital' and was applied to the city in 1403, during the Ming dynasty, to distinguish it from Nanjing, the 'Southern Capital'. The older English spelling Peking was used by the Jesuit missionary Martino Martini in an atlas published in Amsterdam in 1655. Over the past 3,000 years the city has had numerous other names.

The earliest traces of human habitation in the municipality were found in the caves of Dragon Bone Hill near the village of Zhoukoudian, where Peking Man lived. Homo erectus fossils from the caves date to 230,000 to 250,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens lived there more recently, about 27,000 years ago. Neolithic settlements have been found throughout the municipality, including in Wangfujing in central Beijing.

The first walled city in the area was Ji, the capital of the state of Ji, located around the present Guang'anmen area in the south of Xicheng District. During the early Zhou period the settlement was conquered by the state of Yan, which made it its new capital. Its original capital lay 45 kilometres to the southwest in Fangshan District. Yan eventually became one of the seven major states of China in the Warring States period.

Beijing is the capital of China and is governed as a provincial-level municipality with 16 districts. In 2024 its population was about 21.8 million. Its traditional housing consists of siheyuans, courtyard houses, and the narrow alleys between them called hutongs. It has eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Ming Tombs, the Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site and parts of the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. Beijing opera is its best-known traditional form of theatre.
belarus: Belarus is a landlocked country of 207,600 square kilometres, lying between latitudes 51° and 57° N and measuring 560 kilometres from north to south and 650 from west to east. It is relatively flat, with large tracts of marshy land, about 40% forest, and 11,000 lakes.

Three major rivers run through it: the Neman flows west toward the Baltic Sea, the Pripyat flows east to the Dnieper, and the Dnieper flows south toward the Black Sea. The highest point is Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, at 345 metres. About 70% of the radiation from the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighbouring Ukraine entered Belarusian territory, and about a fifth of the land was affected by fallout.

Baltic tribes first permanently settled the region in the 3rd century, and around the 5th century the Slavs took it over, and the gradual assimilation of the Baltic settlers into Slavic culture was peaceful. In the 9th century it became part of Kievan Rus', a vast East Slavic state ruled by the Rurikids, which split into independent principalities on the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054.

The Battle on the Nemiga River in 1067 is considered the founding date of Minsk. The lands avoided the brunt of the 13th-century Mongol invasion and joined the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; the annals affirm an alliance and united foreign policy between Polotsk and Lithuania for decades. The duchy fought alongside Poland against the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410.

By the 14th century the lands had come fully under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, a period lasting 500 years until the partitions of 1792–1795 placed Belarus within the Russian Empire for the first time. The Byelorussian SSR, formed after the Russian Revolution, became a founding republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. After the Polish-Soviet War (1918–1921) Belarus lost almost half its territory to Poland, and in the Second World War it lost about a quarter of its population and half of its economic resources. Many prominent Belarusian intellectuals were exiled or killed in Stalinist purges in the 1930s.

Belarus proclaimed its sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and gained independence on 25 August 1991. Belarus and Russia signed a treaty in 2000 forming the Union State. The official languages are Russian and Belarusian. Francysk Skaryna's Bible, published between 1517 and 1525, was the first book printed in Belarus or anywhere in Eastern Europe.
belgium: Belgium covers 30,689 square kilometres in the Low Countries, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, France and the North Sea. It has three main geographical regions: the coastal plain in the northwest, with sand dunes and polders; the central plateau, a slowly rising landscape of fertile valleys and the sandy plain of the Campine; and the forested, rugged Ardennes in the southeast. The highest point is the Signal de Botrange, at 694 metres. The climate is maritime temperate, with significant precipitation in all seasons.

In his account of the conquest of Gaul, Julius Caesar described the Belgae as inhabiting northern Gaul between the Seine and Marne rivers and the Rhine, and as the bravest of the Gauls. The northernmost tribes, including the Menapii, Nervii and Atuatuci, held most of modern Belgium. After Caesar's conquests the Roman province of Gallia Belgica covered most of northern Gaul, and the eastern part of modern Belgium lay in Germania Inferior. As Roman central government collapsed, the provinces were inhabited by Romanised populations and Germanic-speaking Franks, who came to dominate military and political life.

The region was later part of the Carolingian Empire, the Holy Roman Empire and the Burgundian Netherlands, and was ruled by Habsburg Spain (1556–1714), the Austrian Habsburgs (1714–1794) and Revolutionary France (1794–1815). Most of it joined the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Being contested by so many powers gave Belgium the name the Battlefield of Europe.

An independent Belgium was established in 1830 after the Belgian Revolution. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and mining and steelmaking in Liège Province and around Charleroi made it one of the three most industrialised nations in the world from 1830 to 1910, although Flanders suffered famine from 1846 to 1850.

Belgium is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a federal state of three regions, Flanders, Wallonia and the Brussels-Capital Region, with Dutch-speaking, French-speaking and small German-speaking communities. Tensions between Dutch-speakers and French-speakers rose in the second half of the twentieth century and led to reforms that turned a unitary state into a federal one between 1970 and 1993. After the 2010 federal election the country went a record 589 days without forming a government. Brussels hosts the seats of several European Union institutions, and the country's colonies, the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi, became independent between 1960 and 1962.
belgrade: Belgrade lies 116.75 m above sea level at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers, at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Its historical core, Kalemegdan, stands on the right banks of both rivers. Since the 19th century the city has expanded to the south and east, and after World War II New Belgrade was built on the left bank of the Sava, connecting Belgrade with Zemun. The name in Serbian, Beograd, means White City.

Chipped stone tools found in Zemun show that nomadic foragers lived around Belgrade in the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic eras. The first farmers belonged to the Neolithic Starčevo culture, which flourished between 6200 and 5200 BCE, and the Vinča culture (5500-4500 BCE) grew out of their settlements and is known for very large settlements. In antiquity Thraco-Dacians inhabited the region, and after 279 BCE Celts settled the city and named it Singidūn. The Romans conquered it under Augustus and awarded it city rights in the mid-2nd century.

Slavs settled the city in the 520s.
